analysis.one_liner: Restores contribution limits to super PACs, capping single-source donations at the standard $5,000 PAC limit.
analysis.headline: Sen. Sanders' bill to cap super PAC contributions was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Rules Committee, where it has seen no further action; the bill's own findings note super PACs raised unlimited money from 2,459 committees spending $4.48 billion in 2024.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 2010 court ruling struck down contribution limits for groups that spend independently in elections (super PACs), a single donor can give millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars to a committee supporting a candidate, as long as the committee doesn't formally coordinate with the campaign. This bill would amend campaign finance law so that super PACs are subject to the same contribution cap as every other political committee — the standard $5,000-per-election limit — effectively ending the unlimited-donor model. It took effect the calendar year after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, whose elections would no longer be dominated by a tiny number of mega-donors. The bill's findings note that in 2024 the top 1% of individual super PAC contributors supplied about 97% of all individual super PAC money, and that uncapped contributions create both the risk and the appearance of corruption. Candidates from both parties who cannot tap billionaire donors would also compete on somewhat more equal footing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary voters and candidates without billionaire backers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act so that committees making independent expenditures — super PACs — fall under the same contribution limits that apply to all other political committees, ending the unlimited-donor model created by the 2010 SpeechNow ruling.

The bill's findings argue the cap limits the risk that candidates and donors use super PACs as a conduit for corrupt bargains, since super PAC support is now critical to federal campaigns and bribery routed through a third party is notoriously hard to prosecute.
The findings state that contribution limits would also make it harder for foreign entities to funnel money into U.S. elections through third-party contributors.

Per the bill's findings, independent expenditures grew more than 700% between 2008 and 2020, reaching $4.48 billion in 2024 from 2,459 registered super PACs — spending concentrated in very few hands that this bill would cap.

analysis.who_pays: Super PAC mega-donors — a small group of individuals, corporations, and unions who currently can give unlimited sums — lose their dominant channel of influence. Political committees, consultants, and the advertising ecosystem built around nine-figure super PAC budgets would shrink. Donors who want to keep spending unlimited amounts could still spend their own money directly on independent expenditures, which the bill does not touch.

drawbacks.text: The cap is very likely to face a constitutional challenge: the D.C. Circuit's SpeechNow.org v. FEC decision, which the bill's own findings target, struck down contribution limits on independent-expenditure committees in 2010, and courts have treated contribution limits to such committees as unconstitutional under the Citizens United line of cases — so the bill could be struck down rather than take effect.

Capping super PAC contributions would not cap spending itself: wealthy donors could still spend unlimited personal funds on independent expenditures, and money could shift toward groups that are harder to trace, so the bill limits donor aggregation without fully limiting election spending.

Critics of contribution limits argue that capping super PACs can entrench power that flows through party committees and incumbents, who already have established fundraising networks that smaller outside groups cannot match.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — returning influence over elections from a few hundred mega-donors to the broader public — is real and large, and the cost falls almost entirely on the donors and campaign industries that profit from unlimited giving. The main honest caveats are legal and practical: current court precedent makes the cap vulnerable to being struck down, and money that leaves super PACs could migrate to less transparent channels. Still, as an anti-corruption measure aimed at the largest concentration of money in federal elections, the benefit-to-cost balance favors ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernard Sanders introduced the Abolish Super PACs Act on May 20, 2026.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote has followed.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, giving it a total of two sponsors in the Senate.

The bill's text would apply the standard contribution limits of Section 315(a)(1)(C) to independent expenditure committees, defined as committees making or passing along $5,000 or more in independent expenditures per year, effective the first calendar year after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, super PACs and their unlimited donors: with no committee action and near-total Senate indifference, the unlimited-money system the bill targets remains untouched.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Abolish Super PACs Act and referred it to the Rules and Administration Committee.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since May 2026.

sides.party_line_note: There is no roll-call to measure partisanship; the bill has a single independent sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no Republican support is recorded.

industries.industry: Super PACs and their major donors
industries.note: The bill would strip them of unlimited single-source contributions, capping donations at the standard PAC limit. Their financial interest depends on keeping the uncapped system the bill targets. The bill's findings show the top 1% of individual donors supplied about 97% of individual super PAC money in 2024.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign advertising firms
industries.note: A cap that shrinks the $4.48 billion independent-expenditure marketplace shrinks the consulting, media-buying, and ad-production business built around it. Fewer giant ad buys means less revenue for firms serving super PACs.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no recorded Republican support, and no action from the Rules Committee since referral, the bill is unlikely to advance to a hearing or vote in this Congress. Campaign finance measures of this kind routinely die in committee, and the bill would also face a near-certain constitutional challenge if it ever became law.
